# @ratmath/geo 0.4.0: full documentation

> Geometry for RatMath: Euclidean constructions, theorems checked on exact figures and proved in general, spherical, hyperbolic, projective and finite geometries, symmetry and tilings. From https://ratmath.com/geo/, commit 7ea0c6c. Each page ends with a runnable example; in it, PRINT(...) prints.


---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/index.html

@ratmath/geo

## Geometry where equal means equal

Three points are on a line or they are not, and a floating-point test can only say "nearly". Here coordinates are exact: fractions, or algebraic numbers such as 3​/2 when a compass has been used. So collinear, concyclic and tangent are decided, and a theorem checked on a figure is checked.

### What is here

### A first program

```js
import { triangle, circle, line, meet, rotation, theorems, delaunay, pick, metric } from "@ratmath/geo";

const t = triangle([0, 0], [4, 0], [1, 3]);
String(t.orthocenter);                      // "(1, 1)"
String(t.incenter);                         // exact, with nested square roots
theorems.feuerbach(t).holds;                // true: the nine-point circle touches the incircle
meet(circle([0, 0], [1, 0]), circle([1, 0], [0, 0])).map(String);   // ["(1/2, -√3/2)", "(1/2, √3/2)"]
String(rotation([0, 0], "1/6").apply([1, 0]));                      // "(1/2, √3/2)"
delaunay([[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]).cocircular;              // true: decided, not guessed
pick([[0, 0], [5, 0], [0, 5]]);             // { area: 25/2, interior: 6, boundary: 15, holds: true }
metric("taxicab").pi;                       // 4
```

### Numbers

A coordinate is a Core `Rational` whenever it is rational, and otherwise an algebraic number from `@ratmath/algebraic`, which keeps its minimal polynomial and so can be added, compared and tested for zero exactly. Everything a ruler and compass can construct is such a number, and so are the vertices of every regular polygon. Inputs are whole numbers, fractions `"7/2"`, decimals `"0.35"` (meaning 7/20) and square roots `"sqrt(3)/2"`. A JavaScript number that is not whole is refused. `N` exports the arithmetic (`N.add`, `N.sqrt`, `N.cmp`, `N.text`…).

Rational figures stay rational and fast. Figures with square roots are slower, since each comparison works with minimal polynomials; a triangle's incentre and the circles around it take a fraction of a second.

### Projective, finite, solid and symmetric

The [projective plane](https://ratmath.com/geo/projective.html) works in homogeneous coordinates, where cross-ratios and projective maps are exact and Desargues, Pappus, Pascal and Brianchon can be checked on any exact figure. [Finite geometries](https://ratmath.com/geo/finite-geometries.html) are built over algebraic's finite fields, from the seven-point Fano plane up, with their collineation groups. [Polyhedra](https://ratmath.com/geo/polyhedra.html) have exact coordinates in Q(√2) or Q(√5): volumes, dihedral angles, duals and symmetry groups. Plane patterns get their [rosette, frieze or wallpaper group](https://ratmath.com/geo/symmetry.html), and the [tilings page](https://ratmath.com/geo/tilings.html) shows why only 11 of the 21 vertex types of regular polygons tile uniformly. [Pictures of geometry](https://ratmath.com/geo/pictures.html) grows and draws those 11 tilings, draws solids, patterns, finite planes and constructions with RatMath Graphics, and joins geo's exact plane with graphics'.

### The sphere and the hyperbolic plane

On the [sphere](https://ratmath.com/geo/spherical.html) a triangle's angles add up to more than π, and in the [hyperbolic plane](https://ratmath.com/geo/hyperbolic.html) to less; in both, the difference is the area. Points have exact coordinates, distances keep their exact cosine or cosh, and whether an angle is a rational multiple of π is decided, so the octant triangle covers exactly one eighth of the sphere and a triangle with three ideal vertices has area exactly π. The hyperbolic plane is one object seen in four models, with its [isometries classified and its regular tilings](https://ratmath.com/geo/hyperbolic-triangles.html) sized exactly. [The parallel postulate](https://ratmath.com/geo/parallel-postulate.html) is then a count that comes out differently in each geometry.

### Proofs for every figure

A check tests one figure. [General proofs](https://ratmath.com/geo/proofs.html) cover all of them: the coordinates are letters, the hypotheses and conclusion are polynomials, and the proof is one polynomial identity found by Wu's method or a Gröbner basis and then multiplied out to confirm. The Euler line, the nine-point circle, Simson's line, the butterfly theorem, Pappus and Desargues are among the twenty-one proved, each with its degenerate cases listed.

```js
import { proofs, configuration } from "@ratmath/geo";

const p = proofs.eulerLine();
p.proved;                                  // true, for every triangle
p.conditions.map((c) => c.meaning);       // ["A, B, C are not collinear"]
p.replay();                                // true: the certificate multiplies out
```

Every phase of the [roadmap for this package](https://github.com/ratmath/ratmath/blob/main/docs/design/library-roadmap.md#11-a-geometry-package-ratmathgeo) is now built. The [RatMath Shelf](https://ratmath.com/shelf/) page lists what exists across all the libraries.

### Try it

```js
const t = triangle([0, 0], [4, 0], [1, 3]);
PRINT("centroid", String(t.centroid), " circumcentre", String(t.circumcenter), " orthocentre", String(t.orthocenter));
PRINT("incentre", String(t.incenter));
PRINT("area", N.text(t.area), " circumradius", N.text(t.circumradius), " cos A", N.text(t.cosines.A));
for (const name of ["eulerLine", "ninePointCircle", "feuerbach", "napoleon"]) PRINT(theorems[name](t).theorem + ":", theorems[name](t).statement, "→", theorems[name](t).holds);
PRINT("two unit circles meet at", meet(circle([0, 0], [1, 0]), circle([1, 0], [0, 0])).join(" and "));
PRINT("octant triangle: excess", striangle([1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]).excess.text, "  ideal hyperbolic triangle: area", htriangle(ideal(1, 0), ideal(0, 1), ideal(-1, 0)).area.text);
plan.map((p) => `${p.phase}. ${p.contents}`)
```

Reference

## Everything in the library

Every export of `@ratmath/geo`, with what it takes and what it returns. A point goes in as `[x, y]` or a `Point`; a coordinate is a whole number, a fraction or decimal string, a string such as `"sqrt(3)/2"`, a Core `Rational` or an algebraic number. A JavaScript number that is not whole is refused.

### Numbers

| Export | What it does |

| num(x) | An exact number from any of the forms above: a Rational when rational, otherwise an algebraic number. |

| N | Arithmetic on those numbers: add, sub, mul, div, neg, sq, sqrt, sign, isZero, cmp, eq, abs, min, max, sum, isRational, toNumber, text(a, digits), enclose(a, bits), cosPi(q), sinPi(q). |

| GeoError | What the library throws, with a code: inexact, bad-number, bad-figure, division, sqrt and others. |

### Points, lines, circles

| Export | What it does |

| point(x, y), Point | A point. Methods: equals, plus, minus, times(k), toNumbers(). |

| line(p, q), line(a, b, c), Line | The line through two points, or ax+by+c=0. Methods: contains(p), at(p), equals; fields a, b, c, direction. |

| circle(centre, through), Circle | The circle with a centre through a point. Fields: center, radius, radius2. Methods: contains(p), power(p), equals. |

| distance(p, q), distance2(p, q), midpoint(p, q) | Exact distance, its square, and the midpoint. |

| dot(u, v), cross(u, v), orientation(p, q, r) | Products of vectors; +1 for a left turn, −1 for a right turn, 0 on a line. |

| collinear(...points), concyclic(...points) | Exact tests. |

| parallel(l, m), perpendicular(l, m), concurrent(l, m, n) | Exact tests on lines. |

| parallelThrough(l, p), perpendicularThrough(l, p), perpendicularBisector(p, q) | Lines. |

| angleBisector(a, v, b, { external }) | The bisector of the angle at v. |

| foot(p, l), reflect(p, l) | Foot of the perpendicular, and mirror image. |

| meet(f, g) | The points common to two lines, a line and a circle, or two circles, as an array. |

| tangents(c, p), circumcircle(a, b, c) | Tangent lines from a point; the circle through three points. |

| regularPolygon(n, { center, vertex }) | The vertices, exact for every n. |

| construction(given), Construction | A recorded ruler-and-compass construction: line, circle, meet, get, count. See Constructions. |

### Measurement

| name | what it gives |

| angleSum(n), interiorAngle(n), exteriorAngle(n) | (n − 2)·180, (n − 2)·180/n and 360/n, in degrees, exactly |

| line.slope, line.intercept, line.toSlopeIntercept(), line.toPointSlope(p) | slope and intercept (null when vertical); "y = mx + b" and "y − y₀ = m(x − x₀)" |

| slopeIntercept(p, q), pointSlope(p, m) | { slope, intercept, text, line } of the line through two points; the line through p with slope m |

| tangentLength(circle, p) | √(power of p) |

| circleFromEquation(text \| [A..F]), conicCoefficients(...) | the circle by completing the square; the six coefficients of a conic |

| box(a, b, c), cylinder(r, h), cone(r, h), sphere(r) | a box as a Polyhedron; the round solids' volume and areas as multiples of π |

| similar(k \| { lengths \| areas \| volumes }) | { scale, length, area, volume } ratios |

### Conic sections

| name | what it gives |

| conicProperties(text \| [A, B, C, D, E, F]), conic.properties() | type (degenerate kinds stop there); for an ellipse or hyperbola center, a, b, c, eccentricity, axes, vertices, coVertices, foci, directrices, asymptotes, standardForm; for a parabola vertex, focus, focalLength, axis, directrix, latusRectum |

### Vectors and planes in space

| name | what it gives |

| vector(x, y, z) | dot, cross, norm, norm2, unit, angle, projectOnto, componentAlong, isParallel, isOrthogonal, add, sub, scale |

| tripleProduct(u, v, w) | u·(v × w), the signed volume |

| line3(p, q), new Line3(point, direction) | at(t), contains, distance |

| plane(p, q, r), plane(p, { normal }), plane({ coefficients }) | equation, coefficients, contains, distance, foot, angle, meet (a line or a plane), isParallel |

### Triangles

| Member of triangle(a, b, c) | What it is |

| sides, sides2, area, perimeter, cosines, degrees, classify() | Measurements. Side a is opposite vertex A. |

| centroid, circumcenter, orthocenter, incenter, excenters, ninePointCenter, symmedian | Centres. See Triangle centres. |

| barycentric(u, v, w) | The point with those weights on A, B, C. |

| circumcircle, incircle, excircles, ninePointCircle, inradius, circumradius | Circles. |

| medians, altitudes, feet, bisectors, eulerLine | Lines and feet of altitudes. |

### Transformations

| Export | What it does |

| identity(), translation(v), rotation(centre, turn), reflection(l), glide(l, v), dilation(centre, k), affine(matrix, vector) | A Transform. A rotation's turn is a fraction of a full turn, as a string. |

| Transform | apply(figure), compose(other), inverse(), equals, determinant, isSimilarity(), isIsometry(), fixed(), classify(). |

| inversion(c) | Inversion in a circle: apply to a point, a line or a circle. |

### Checked theorems

| theorems.… | Takes |

| pythagoras, eulerLine, ninePointCircle, feuerbach, napoleon, concurrency, heron | a triangle |

| ceva, menelaus | a triangle and points D, E, F on BC, CA, AB |

| simson | a triangle and a point |

| ptolemy, varignon | four points |

| thales | a circle and three points on it |

| powerOfPoint | a circle, a point and two lines through it |

| pentagon | nothing |

Each returns { theorem, statement, holds } and the quantities it compared. See [Checked theorems](https://ratmath.com/geo/theorems.html).

### General proofs

| Name | What it is |

| configuration(name) | A figure in coordinates, to state a theorem about. Its methods make points, give the polynomials of geometric properties, and prove. |

| T.at(name, x, y), T.free(name), T.parameter(name) | A point with given coordinates (numbers, parameter names, or expressions); a point with two free coordinates; a free number. |

| T.on(name, P => condition, { free }), T.where(name, P => [c1, c2]), T.unknown(name, v => condition) | A point with one free coordinate and one condition; a point fixed by two conditions; a number fixed by an equation. |

| T.midpoint, intersection, foot, reflection, parallelogram, circumcenter, orthocenter, centroid, tritangentCenter, onLine, onCircumcircle, otherIntersection | Constructions. Lines are pairs of points: T.intersection("P", [A, B], [C, D]). |

| T.collinear, parallel, perpendicular, equidistant, equalLength, onCircle, concyclic, concurrent, rightAngle, equalAngle, tangent, isMidpoint, equal | Predicates: the polynomial (GeoExpr) that vanishes when the property holds. |

| T.distance2, area2, dot, cross, number; e.add, sub, mul, neg, pow | Quantities, and arithmetic on expressions. |

| T.prove(conclusion, { method, timeLimit, maxPairs, instance }) | A Proof. method is "wu", "groebner" or "auto". A list of conclusions gives a Proof with parts. |

| T.instance(conclusion), T.describe(), T.parameters, T.unknowns, T.hypotheses, T.points | One figure tried: { parameters, solutions, holdsAt }; the figure as text; the variables and hypotheses. |

| proof.proved, proof.method, proof.replay() | Whether an identity was found and multiplied out; by which method; multiply it out again. |

| proof.identity | { ring, multiplier, power, cofactors, hypotheses, conclusion } with multiplier · conclusion^power = Σ cofactors[i] · hypotheses[i], as polynomials of @ratmath/structures. |

| proof.conditions | The degenerate cases: [{ polynomial, text, meaning }]. The proof covers every figure at which none vanishes. |

| proof.explain({ cofactors }), proof.parts, proof.instance, proof.size, proof.ms | The proof as text; one proof per conclusion; the figure tried when not proved; size of the certificate; time taken. |

| provable, proofs.(options), proofs.all(options), proofs.setup(id) | The classical theorems proved in general: thales, pythagoras, isosceles, midline, medians, altitudes, bisectors, eulerLine, ninePointCircle, orthocentreReflection, tritangent, varignon, parallelogram, inscribedAngle, chords, simson, butterfly, pappus, desargues, gaussLine, napoleon. |

See [General proofs](https://ratmath.com/geo/proofs.html).

### Discrete and other geometries

| Export | What it does |

| convexHull(points) | The hull, counter-clockwise, without points inside edges. |

| onSegment(a, b, p), segmentIntersection(a, b, c, d) | An exact test, and { meets, kind, point }: kind is "none", "cross", "touch" or "overlap" (then with from and to). |

| polygon(vertices), Polygon | area, signedArea, perimeter, centroid, edges, isConvex(), isSimple(), locate(p), contains(p), triangulate(), clip(convex). |

| inCircle(a, b, c, d) | The sign of d against the circle through a, b, c. |

| delaunay(points), voronoi(points) | { points, triangles, edges, cocircular } and { points, vertices, cells, edges, cocircular }. See Computational geometry. |

| closestPair(points) | { points, distance2, distance }. |

| latticePointsOn(p, q), pick(vertices), isVisible(x, y), visiblePoints(n) | See Lattice geometry. |

| metric(name) | "taxicab", "chebyshev" or "euclidean": distance, circle, pi, bisector, ellipse. See Taxicab geometry. |

| plan | The phases still to come, each { phase, contents, estimate }. |

### Projective and finite geometry

| Export | What it does |

| ppoint, pline, lineAtInfinity, PPoint, PLine | Points and lines in homogeneous coordinates; dual swaps them. See The projective plane. |

| join, meetLines, collinearP, concurrentP | Incidence, exactly. |

| crossRatio, harmonicConjugate | The projective invariant of four collinear points. |

| projectivity(matrix), projectivityFrom(from, to), Projectivity | Projective maps: apply, compose, inverse, isAffine. |

| conicThrough(points), Conic | Conics: contains, polar, pole, tangentAt, transform, classify. |

| desargues, pappus, pascal, brianchon | The classical theorems checked on a figure. |

| projectivePlane(q), affinePlane(q), fano(), incidence(lines) | Finite planes and incidence structures: axioms, designParameters, parallels, completion, collineations, collineationGroup. See Finite geometries. |

### The sphere and the hyperbolic plane

| Export | What it does |

| angle(x), Angle, turnsOfCos(c), piTimes(k) | Angles with exact cosine and sine; turns is the fraction of a full turn or null, decided exactly; value(digits) encloses the radians. See Spherical geometry. |

| Length | A hyperbolic length by its exact cosh and sinh: exp, text, value(digits), add, double, half. |

| spoint, latLon, fromStereographic, northPole, SPoint | Points of the unit sphere: antipode, distanceTo, latLon, stereographic. |

| greatCircle(P, Q), equator(), GreatCircle | contains, poles, meet, angleWith, perpendicularThrough, distanceTo, reflection, parallelsThrough. |

| striangle(A, B, C), STriangle, lune | sides, angles, excess, area, fractionOfSphere, polar, classify(), checks(). |

| scircle(centre, through), SCircle | radius, circumference and area as multiples of π. |

| srotation(axis, turns), antipodalMap(), SIsometry | apply, then, inverse, classify(): rotation, reflection or rotary reflection. |

| hpoint(x, y), fromKlein, fromHalfPlane, fromHyperboloid, horigin, HPoint | A point of the hyperbolic plane: disc, klein, halfPlane, hyperboloid, distanceTo. See The hyperbolic plane. |

| ideal(x, y), HIdeal | A point at infinity. |

| hline(a, b), hbisector, hmidpoint, HLine | ends, disc, klein, halfPlane, distanceTo, foot, perpendicularThrough, relation, reflection, parallelsThrough. |

| hcircle(centre, through), horocycle(ideal, p), HCircle | radius, circumference, area, and the Euclidean circle in the disc. |

| htriangle(A, B, C), HTriangle | sides, angles, defect, area, checks(); vertices may be ideal. See Hyperbolic triangles, motions, tilings. |

| hreflection, hrotation, hhalfTurn, htranslation, HIsometry | apply, then, inverse, classify(), toMobius(). |

| schlafli(p, q), hyperbolicTiling(p, q) | The regular tiling {p, q}: its geometry and exact tile; a patch of tiles. |

| parallelPostulate({ q }) | Playfair's postulate counted in five geometries. See The parallel postulate. |

| hyperbolicFigure(items, { model }), hyperbolicTilingFigure(p, q, { layers, model }) | Figures in the Poincaré disc, the Klein disc or the half-plane. |

### Solids, symmetry and tilings

| Export | What it does |

| polyhedron(points), Polyhedron, solids, prism(n) | Convex polyhedra with proved faces: euler, volume, surfaceArea, dihedralCosines, dual, symmetry. See Polyhedra. |

| figureSymmetry(points) | The rosette group Cₙ or Dₙ of a finite figure. See Symmetry groups. |

| friezeGroup({ points, period }), friezes | One of the seven frieze groups. |

| wallpaperGroup({ gram, points }), wallpaper | One of the seventeen wallpaper groups, with the flowchart's steps; patterns for each. |

| polygonAngle, vertexTypes, uniformTiling, regularTilings | Tilings by regular polygons. See Tilings. |

### Try it

```js
// A little of each part.
const t = triangle([0, 0], [4, 0], [1, 3]);
PRINT("area", N.text(t.area), " incentre", String(t.incenter), " Euler line", String(t.eulerLine));
PRINT("rotation by a sixth of a turn sends (1, 0) to", String(rotation([0, 0], "1/6").apply(point(1, 0))));
PRINT("Feuerbach holds:", theorems.feuerbach(t).holds);
PRINT("hull:", convexHull([[0, 0], [4, 0], [5, 3], [2, 5], [-1, 3], [2, 2]]).join(" "));
PRINT("taxicab π =", N.text(metric("taxicab").pi));
PRINT("sphere:", striangle([1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 0], [1, 1, 1]).excess.text, " hyperbolic:", horigin().distanceTo(hpoint("1/2", 0)).text);
plan.map((p) => p.phase)
```

Explore

## Explore

Type the corners of a triangle, or a list of points. The pictures are drawn from exact coordinates, and the theorems are checked exactly for the figure you gave. Further down: a solid with its exact measurements and symmetry group, and a wallpaper pattern named by its group.

### A triangle

A
B
C

Each corner is two exact numbers separated by a comma: `1/2`, `0.35` and `sqrt(3)` all work. The picture shows the circumcircle, the incircle, the nine-point circle and the Euler line through O, G and H. Try `0, 0`, `2, 0`, `1, sqrt(3)`, where the centres coincide.

### A set of points

Points

Points are separated by semicolons. The outline is the convex hull and the inner lines are the Delaunay triangulation; the two highlighted points are the closest pair.

### A solid

Solid
its dual
Turn

The solids with √5 in their coordinates take a moment, since every face is proved with exact algebraic numbers.

### A wallpaper pattern

Group
Seed point

The pattern is made by applying the group's generators to the seed point and two companions of other colours, then classified again from scratch by the flowchart.

### A hyperbolic triangle

A
B
C
Model

The points are given in the Poincaré disc (inside the unit circle) and shown in the model chosen. The angles have exact cosines; the defect, π minus their sum, is the area.

### A regular tiling {p, q}

p
q
Steps

Regular p-gons, q at each corner. The page says which geometry the tiling lives in; a hyperbolic one is drawn in the Poincaré disc, from floats, with the tile's exact size beside it.

### Try it

```js
// The page above, as code.
const t = triangle([0, 0], [6, 0], [1, 4]);
PRINT("O", String(t.circumcenter), " G", String(t.centroid), " H", String(t.orthocenter));
PRINT("Euler line:", String(t.eulerLine), "  checked:", theorems.eulerLine(t).holds);
const pts = [[0, 0], [6, 0], [7, 4], [3, 7], [-1, 4], [2, 2], [4, 3], [3, 1]];
PRINT("hull:", convexHull(pts).join(" "));
PRINT("closest pair:", closestPair(pts).points.join(" and "));
PRINT(delaunay(pts).triangles.length, "Delaunay triangles");
const ht = htriangle([0, 0], ["1/2", 0], ["1/4", "1/2"]);
PRINT("hyperbolic triangle: angles", ht.angles.A.text, ht.angles.B.text, ht.angles.C.text, " area", ht.area.text);
const s73 = schlafli(7, 3);
`{7, 3} is ${s73.geometry}: tile area ${s73.tileArea.text}, edge ${s73.edge.text}`
```

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/constructions.html

Topic

## Points, lines, circles and constructions

The Euclidean plane has three kinds of object and two tools. Everything the tools can make has coordinates that are exact numbers, and this page is about those.

```js
const l = line([0, 0], [2, 1]);              // or line(a, b, c) for ax + by + c = 0
const c = circle([0, 0], { radius: 1 });     // or circle(centre, pointOnIt)
meet(l, c);                                  // 0, 1 or 2 points, exact
perpendicularBisector([0, 0], [4, 0]);       // x − 2 = 0
regularPolygon(5);                           // five exact vertices on the unit circle

const k = construction({ A: [0, 0], B: [1, 0] });
k.circle("a", "A", "B").circle("b", "B", "A").meet(["C", "D"], "a", "b").line("m", "C", "D");
String(k.get("C"));                          // "(1/2, -√3/2)"
```

### What the tools add

A ruler draws the line through two known points; a compass draws the circle with a known centre through a known point. New points appear where these meet. Two lines meet where two linear equations hold, which needs only +, −, ×, ÷. A line and a circle, or two circles, meet where a quadratic equation holds, which needs one square root more. So starting from rational points, every constructible coordinate is built from rationals by the four operations and square roots, however deep the nesting. These are algebraic numbers, and `meet` returns them exactly: the vertex of the regular pentagon is (4−1+5​​,410+25​​​).

Two circles meet on their radical axis, the line left when one circle's equation is subtracted from the other's, so that case reduces to a line and a circle.

### Predicates

Because the numbers are exact, so are the questions asked of them: `collinear`, `concyclic`, `concurrent`, `parallel`, `perpendicular`, `orientation` (left turn, right turn or straight), `circle.power(p)` (negative inside, zero on, positive outside). None of them takes a tolerance.

### A construction as a list of steps

`construction(given)` records a construction the way it is written in a textbook. Each step names what it makes: `line(name, P, Q)` uses the ruler, `circle(name, centre, through)` the compass (a third argument carries the radius |PQ| to another centre), and `meet(names, f, g)` marks intersections. `count` says how many times each tool was used, `String(k)` prints the steps, and `get(name)` returns any object with its exact coordinates.

### Regular polygons

`regularPolygon(n)` uses the exact values of cos(2πk/n) and sin(2πk/n). For n = 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17, … these are nested square roots, which is Gauss's theorem on which polygons are constructible. For n = 7 or 9 they are algebraic numbers of degree 3 that no nest of square roots expresses: still exact here, but out of the compass's reach.

| call | returns |

| point(x, y), line(P, Q), line(a, b, c), circle(centre, through \| { radius }) | Point, Line, Circle |

| meet(f, g) | Point or null (two lines); Point[] ordered by x then y |

| distance, distance2, midpoint, foot(P, l), reflect(P, l) | exact numbers and Points |

| parallelThrough(l, P), perpendicularThrough(l, P), perpendicularBisector(P, Q), angleBisector(A, V, B) | Line |

| circumcircle(A, B, C), tangents(circle, P), regularPolygon(n, { center, vertex }) | Circle, Line[], Point[] |

| collinear, concyclic, concurrent, parallel, perpendicular, orientation | exact predicates |

| construction(given).line(…).circle(…).meet(…) | Construction: get(name), steps, count |

### Try it

```js
// Bisect a segment, the way Euclid does.
const k = construction({ A: [0, 0], B: [1, 0] });
k.circle("a", "A", "B").circle("b", "B", "A").meet(["C", "D"], "a", "b").line("m", "C", "D").line("AB", "A", "B").meet("M", "m", "AB");
PRINT(String(k));
PRINT("C =", String(k.get("C")), " M =", String(k.get("M")), " tools:", JSON.stringify(k.count));
PRINT("ABC is equilateral:", N.eq(distance2(k.get("A"), k.get("C")), distance2(k.get("A"), k.get("B"))));

PRINT("pentagon:", regularPolygon(5).join("  "));
PRINT("a vertex of the heptagon:", String(regularPolygon(7)[1]), "(exact, but not a nest of square roots)");
const c = circle([0, 0], { radius: 1 });
PRINT("tangents from (2, 0):", tangents(c, [2, 0]).join("   and   "));
concyclic([1, 0], [0, 1], [-1, 0], ["3/5", "-4/5"])
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/measurement.html

Topic

## Measurement: angles, lines, circles, solids

The everyday measurements of school geometry, each exact: the angles of a polygon, a line written as y = mx + b, the length of a tangent, the centre and radius hidden in an equation, and the volumes and areas of solids, with π kept as a symbol.

### Angles of a polygon

A polygon with n sides cuts into n−2 triangles from one vertex, so its interior angles add to (n−2)⋅180∘. A regular one has each interior angle (n−2)⋅180∘/n, and each exterior angle 360∘/n: walking round the polygon turns you once.

```js
angleSum(8);        // 1080 (degrees)
interiorAngle(8);   // 135
exteriorAngle(8);   // 45
interiorAngle(7);   // 900/7, exactly
```

### Forms of a line

geo stores a line as ax+by+c=0, which covers vertical lines too. Every line that is not vertical has a slope m=−a/b and a y-intercept −c/b, and can be written in slope–intercept form y=mx+b or in point–slope form y−y0​=m(x−x0​) through any of its points.

```js
const l = line([-2, 5], [4, -7]);
l.slope;                    // -2
l.toSlopeIntercept();       // "y = -2x + 1"
l.toPointSlope([-2, 5]);    // "y - 5 = -2(x + 2)"
slopeIntercept([0, 0], [2, 1]).text;          // "y = (1/2)x"
pointSlope([1, 2], "3/4").toSlopeIntercept(); // "y = (3/4)x + 5/4"
```

### Tangent length

The radius to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent, so from a point at distance d from the centre the tangent segment has length d2−r2​: the square root of the point's power with respect to the circle.

```js
tangentLength(circle([0, 0], [5, 0]), [13, 0]);   // 12
```

### A circle from its equation

Completing the square turns x2+y2+Dx+Ey+F=0 into (x+D/2)2+(y+E/2)2=(D2+E2)/4−F. `circleFromEquation` reads the equation as text (any common factor, either side of the equals sign) or as the six coefficients of a general conic, and says so when the equation is a single point or has no points at all.

```js
const c = circleFromEquation("x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0");
c.center;    // (3, -2)
c.radius;    // 5
circleFromEquation("x^2 + y^2 + 1 = 0");   // refused: no real point (r² < 0)
```

### Solids

`box(a, b, c)` is an exact [polyhedron](https://ratmath.com/geo/polyhedra.html), so it has a volume, a surface area, faces and edges. The round solids report their measures as multiples of π: a cylinder has volume πr2h and surface 2πr(r+h), a cone 31​πr2h and πr(r+s) with slant s=r2+h2​, a sphere 34​πr3 and 4πr2.

```js
box(4, 5, 6).surfaceArea;   // 148
cylinder(3, 5).volume.text; // "45·π"
cone(3, 4).surfaceArea.text;// "24·π" (slant 5)
sphere(3).volume.text;      // "36·π"
```

Similar figures with scale factor k have areas in the ratio k2 and volumes in the ratio k3. `similar` takes k, or two corresponding lengths, areas or volumes, and returns all three ratios.

```js
similar({ volumes: [8, 27] });   // { scale: 3/2, area: 9/4, volume: 27/8 }
```

### Try it

```js
// The angles of regular polygons, and the tilings they allow
for (const n of [3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12]) PRINT(`${n} sides: each angle ${interiorAngle(n)}°, ${new Rational(360n).divide(interiorAngle(n))} fit round a point`);

// The line through two points, three ways
const l = line([-2, 5], [4, -7]);
PRINT(String(l), " | ", l.toSlopeIntercept(), " | ", l.toPointSlope([4, -7]));

// A circle hidden in an equation, and a tangent from outside it
const c = circleFromEquation("x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0");
PRINT("centre", String(c.center), "radius", String(c.radius), " tangent from (15, 3):", String(tangentLength(c, [15, 3])));

// Archimedes: a sphere is two thirds of its cylinder, in volume and in area
const S = sphere(1), C = cylinder(1, 2);
PRINT("sphere", S.volume.text, S.surfaceArea.text, " cylinder", C.volume.text, C.surfaceArea.text);
box(4, 5, 6).surfaceArea
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/triangles.html

Topic

## Triangles and their centres

A triangle has a great many notable points. The classical ones are here with exact coordinates, along with the circles and lines that go with them.

```js
const t = triangle([0, 0], [4, 0], [1, 3]);
t.centroid; t.circumcenter; t.orthocenter; t.incenter; t.ninePointCenter; t.symmedian;
t.circumcircle; t.incircle; t.excircles.A; t.ninePointCircle;
t.eulerLine; t.medians.A; t.altitudes.B; t.bisectors.C;
t.area; t.sides; t.cosines; t.classify();   // { angles: "acute", sides: "scalene" }
t.barycentric(1, 2, 3);                     // any centre from its weights
```

### Barycentric weights

Every point of the plane is a weighted average of the vertices, (uA+vB+wC)/(u+v+w), and each classical centre has simple weights in terms of the side lengths a, b, c (opposite A, B, C):

| centre | weights | is where |

| centroid G | 1 : 1 : 1 | the medians meet |

| incentre I | a : b : c | the angle bisectors meet; centre of the inscribed circle |

| excentres | −a : b : c and so on | centres of the circles touching one side and two extensions |

| symmedian point | a² : b² : c² | the reflections of the medians in the bisectors meet |

The circumcentre O (perpendicular bisectors) and orthocentre H (altitudes) are found as intersections of lines. For a triangle with rational vertices G, O, H, the nine-point centre and the symmedian point are rational. The incentre is not in general, because the side lengths are square roots: for the triangle above each coordinate has degree 4 or 8 over the rationals and is printed in digits, but it is held exactly, which is how [Feuerbach's theorem](https://ratmath.com/geo/theorems.html) can be checked on it.

### Measures

`area` is half the cross product, rational for rational vertices. `sides` are exact lengths and `sides2` their squares. The angles are given by their cosines, which are exact algebraic numbers; `degrees` gives ordinary numbers for reading. `classify()` decides acute, right or obtuse from the sign of a2+b2−c2 for the longest side, exactly, so a triangle is "right" only when it is.

The inradius is 2⋅area/perimeter and the circumradius the radius of the circle through the vertices; Euler's relation OI2=R(R−2r) connects them and can be tested with `N.eq`.

| property | value |

| A, B, C, vertices, sides, sides2, area, perimeter, cosines, degrees | the figure and its measures |

| centroid, circumcenter, orthocenter, incenter, excenters, ninePointCenter, symmedian, barycentric(u, v, w) | Points |

| circumcircle, incircle, excircles, ninePointCircle, circumradius, inradius | Circles and radii |

| medians, altitudes, bisectors, feet, eulerLine | Lines (by vertex) and Points |

| classify() | { angles, sides } |

### Try it

```js
const t = triangle([0, 0], [4, 0], [1, 3]);
for (const name of ["centroid", "circumcenter", "orthocenter", "ninePointCenter", "symmedian", "incenter"]) PRINT(name.padEnd(16), String(t[name]));
PRINT("Euler line:", String(t.eulerLine));
PRINT("sides:", Object.values(t.sides).map((s) => N.text(s)).join(", "), " area:", N.text(t.area));
PRINT("cosines:", Object.values(t.cosines).map((s) => N.text(s)).join(", "), " degrees:", Object.values(t.degrees).map((d) => d.toFixed(3)).join(", "));
const [O, I, R, r] = [t.circumcenter, t.incenter, t.circumradius, t.inradius];
PRINT("Euler's relation OI² = R(R − 2r):", N.eq(distance2(O, I), N.mul(R, N.sub(R, N.mul(num(2), r)))));
const right = triangle([0, 0], [4, 0], [0, 3]);
PRINT("3-4-5:", JSON.stringify(right.classify()), " incircle:", String(right.incircle), " excentre:", String(right.excenters.A));
triangle([0, 0], [2, 0], [1, "sqrt(3)"]).classify()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/transformations.html

Topic

## Transformations

An isometry of the plane is one of four things: a translation, a rotation, a reflection or a glide reflection. With exact matrices the classification is a computation, and composing two maps and asking what you got is the quickest way to learn it.

```js
const r = rotation([1, 1], "1/4");               // a quarter turn about (1, 1)
String(r.apply([2, 1]));                         // "(1, 2)"
const m = reflection(line([0, 0], [1, 1]));
m.compose(reflection(line([0, 0], [1, 0]))).classify();   // a rotation by 90° about the origin
glide(line([0, 0], [1, 0]), [3, 0]).classify();  // { kind: "glide reflection", axis, vector }
dilation([0, 0], 2).compose(r).classify().kind;  // "spiral similarity"
inversion(circle([0, 0], { radius: 1 })).apply(line([2, 0], [2, 1]));   // a circle through the centre
```

### Exact angles

A rotation matrix needs a cosine and a sine. Given as a fraction of a full turn, `rotation(c, "1/6")`, they are the exact algebraic values (21​ and 23​​ for a sixth of a turn). Or give any exact pair with cos2+sin2=1, such as `{ cos: "3/5", sin: "4/5" }`, which is checked. Rotating by a sixth of a turn six times gives back exactly the identity.

### Classifying

Every map here is p↦Mp+t. `classify()` looks at M:

- MTM=I: an isometry. With determinant +1 it is a translation (M = I) or a rotation, whose centre is the one fixed point. With determinant −1 it is a reflection if it has a line of fixed points, and otherwise a glide reflection: a reflection followed by a slide along the mirror.

- MTM=k2I: a similarity with ratio k. It has exactly one fixed point, its centre: a dilation, a spiral similarity (dilation and rotation), or a dilative reflection.

- otherwise an affine map: lines stay lines and parallels stay parallel, but angles change; the determinant is the factor by which areas are multiplied.

`fixed()` returns the fixed points: a point, a line, the whole plane or none.

Two facts worth trying: reflections in two lines that meet compose to a rotation about the meeting point through twice the angle between them, and in two parallel lines to a translation through twice the distance. So every isometry is a product of at most three reflections.

### Inversion

Inversion in a circle with centre O and radius r sends p to the point p′ on the ray Op with ∣Op∣⋅∣Op′∣=r2. It swaps inside and outside, fixes the circle, and sends lines and circles to lines and circles: a line through O to itself, a line missing O to a circle through O, and a circle through O to a line. `inversion(c).apply(figure)` returns the image exactly.

| call | returns |

| translation(v), rotation(centre, turn \| { cos, sin }), reflection(line), glide(line, v), dilation(centre, k), affine(M, t), identity() | Transform |

| T.apply(point \| line \| circle \| triangle \| points) | the image |

| T.compose(U), T.inverse(), T.equals(U), T.determinant | T after U; the inverse |

| T.isIsometry(), T.isSimilarity(), T.fixed(), T.classify() | { kind, center, axis, vector, cos, sin, ratio, … } |

| inversion(circle).apply(point \| line \| circle) | the image |

### Try it

```js
const a = reflection(line([0, 0], [1, 0]));
const b = reflection(line([0, 0], [1, "sqrt(3)"]));       // a mirror at 60° to the first
const two = b.compose(a).classify();
PRINT("two mirrors at 60°:", two.kind, "about", String(two.center), "by", two.degrees.toFixed(0) + "°");
const par = reflection(line([0, 2], [1, 2])).compose(a).classify();
PRINT("two parallel mirrors 2 apart:", par.kind, "by", String(par.vector));
const three = reflection(line([0, 0], [0, 1])).compose(reflection(line([0, 2], [1, 2]))).compose(reflection(line([1, 0], [2, 1])));
PRINT("three mirrors:", three.classify().kind, " axis", String(three.classify().axis), " glide", String(three.classify().vector));

const r = rotation([0, 0], "1/6");
let power = identity();
for (let k = 0; k < 6; k++) power = r.compose(power);
PRINT("a sixth of a turn, six times, is exactly the identity:", power.equals(identity()));
const spiral = dilation([1, 0], 2).compose(rotation([0, 0], "1/8")).classify();
PRINT(spiral.kind, "ratio", N.text(spiral.ratio), "centre", String(spiral.center));

const inv = inversion(circle([0, 0], { radius: 1 }));
PRINT("the line x = 2 inverts to:", String(inv.apply(line([2, 0], [2, 1]))));
String(inv.apply(circle([1, 0], { radius: 1 })))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/theorems.html

Topic

## Theorems, checked on exact figures

Each function here takes a figure, builds what a theorem talks about, and tests the conclusion with exact arithmetic. `holds: true` means the statement is true of this figure, with no tolerance involved.

```js
const t = triangle([0, 0], [4, 0], [1, 3]);
theorems.eulerLine(t);        // { theorem, statement, holds: true, O, G, H, … }
theorems.feuerbach(t);        // tangent to the incircle and the three excircles
theorems.ceva(t, D, E, F);    // concurrent exactly when the product of ratios is 1
theorems.ptolemy(A, B, C, D); // equality exactly when the four points are concyclic
```

### What a check is, and is not

A check on one triangle is not a proof for all triangles. It is still worth more than a drawing or a floating-point test, for two reasons. First, the conclusion is an exact equality, so a false statement fails rather than passing within a tolerance. Second, a statement that is an identity between polynomials or algebraic functions of the coordinates and holds at a "generic" exact point is very unlikely to be false. For a proof that covers every figure, see [General proofs](https://ratmath.com/geo/proofs.html), where the coordinates are letters, hypotheses and conclusion become polynomials, and the proof is a certificate.

Several of the functions test both directions. `ceva` reports the product of the ratios and whether the lines are concurrent, and `holds` says these agree, so it is as informative on a figure where the lines miss as on one where they meet. `ptolemy`, `simson` and `thales` work the same way.

| theorems.… | statement checked |

| pythagoras(t) | a² + b² = c² exactly when the triangle is right-angled |

| heron(t) | area² = s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c) |

| concurrency(t) | medians, altitudes and bisectors each meet in a point; G divides the medians 2 : 1 |

| eulerLine(t) | O, G, H are collinear with GH = 2·OG |

| ninePointCircle(t) | nine points on one circle of half the circumradius |

| feuerbach(t) | the nine-point circle touches the incircle and each excircle |

| napoleon(t) | centres of the outer equilateral triangles form an equilateral triangle |

| ceva(t, D, E, F), menelaus(t, D, E, F) | product of signed ratios is 1 (concurrent) or −1 (collinear) |

| simson(t, P) | the feet from P are collinear exactly when P is on the circumcircle |

| ptolemy(A, B, C, D) | AC·BD = AB·CD + BC·DA exactly for cyclic quadrilaterals, ≤ otherwise |

| thales(circle, A, B, P) | angle APB is right exactly when AB is a diameter |

| powerOfPoint(circle, P, l1, l2) | PA·PB is the same on every secant and equals \|PO\|² − r² |

| varignon(A, B, C, D) | midpoints of a quadrilateral form a parallelogram of half the area |

| pentagon() | diagonal : side of the regular pentagon is the golden ratio |

### Why Feuerbach's theorem is the hard one

Two circles touch when the distance between their centres equals the sum or the difference of their radii. The nine-point circle of a rational triangle is rational, but the incentre and inradius involve the three side lengths, each a square root, so the distance is a square root of an expression in three square roots, and the test is whether that equals a difference of two more such numbers. In floating point one sees agreement to fifteen digits. Here the two sides are algebraic numbers and the equality is decided from their minimal polynomials.

### Try it

```js
const t = triangle([0, 0], [4, 0], [1, 3]);
for (const name of ["pythagoras", "heron", "concurrency", "eulerLine", "ninePointCircle", "feuerbach", "napoleon"]) {
  const r = theorems[name](t);
  PRINT(`${r.theorem}: ${r.statement} → ${r.holds}`);
}
const mids = [midpoint(t.B, t.C), midpoint(t.C, t.A), midpoint(t.A, t.B)];
const ceva = theorems.ceva(t, ...mids);
PRINT("Ceva with the midpoints: product", N.text(ceva.product), "concurrent", ceva.concurrent);
const off = theorems.ceva(t, [3, 1], mids[1], [1, 0]);
PRINT("Ceva with other points: product", N.text(off.product), "concurrent", off.concurrent, "→ the theorem still holds:", off.holds);

const cut = line([-1, 1], [5, 2]);
const men = theorems.menelaus(t, meet(cut, line(t.B, t.C)), meet(cut, line(t.C, t.A)), meet(cut, line(t.A, t.B)));
PRINT("Menelaus for a line across the triangle: product", N.text(men.product));
PRINT("Ptolemy, square:", theorems.ptolemy([1, 0], [0, 1], [-1, 0], [0, -1]).equal, " kite off the circle:", theorems.ptolemy([1, 0], [0, 1], [-1, 0], [0, -2]).equal);
const g = theorems.pentagon();
`${g.statement}: ${N.text(g.ratio)}`
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/proofs.html

Topic

## General proofs, by algebra

A [check](https://ratmath.com/geo/theorems.html) tests a theorem on one figure. A proof here covers every figure at once: the coordinates are letters, the hypotheses and the conclusion are polynomials, and the proof is a single polynomial identity that you can multiply out yourself.

Prove a theorem

Theorem
Method
show the cofactors

### From a figure to polynomials

Take Thales' theorem: an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle. Put the centre at the origin and the diameter along the x-axis, from A=(−r,0) to B=(r,0). Nothing is lost by this choice of axes. The third point C=(x,y) is on the circle, and that is the one hypothesis:

h=x2+y2−r2=0.
The conclusion is that CA and CB are perpendicular, so their dot product vanishes:

g=(x+r)(x−r)+y⋅y=x2+y2−r2.
Here g=h, so the conclusion follows from the hypothesis for every r, x and y. That one line is a complete proof of the theorem. Most theorems need more algebra, but the shape is the same.

The coordinates come in three kinds. Some are numbers, fixed by the choice of axes. Some are parameters: r and x above, free to take any value, so that the figure is a general one. The rest are unknowns, tied to the earlier coordinates by the hypotheses: y above. Each unknown comes with one hypothesis.

```js
import { configuration } from "@ratmath/geo";

const T = configuration("Thales");
const O = T.at("O", 0, 0);
const r = T.parameter("r");
const A = T.at("A", r.neg(), 0);
const B = T.at("B", r, 0);
const C = T.on("C", (P) => T.onCircle(P, O, A));    // x free, y tied down by the circle
const proof = T.prove(T.rightAngle(A, C, B));
proof.proved;       // true
proof.method;       // "wu"
proof.replay();     // true: the identity was multiplied out again
```

### What counts as a proof

Let h1​,…,hr​ be the hypotheses and g the conclusion. A proof is an identity between polynomials

d⋅gk=c1​h1​+c2​h2​+⋯+cr​hr​
with a multiplier d that is not the zero polynomial. At any figure where every hi​ is zero the right side is zero, so d⋅gk=0, and wherever d=0 that forces g=0. The identity can be checked by expanding both sides. Nothing about how it was found needs to be trusted, and `proof.replay()` does that expansion each time it is called.

The multiplier matters. Its factors are the degenerate cases, the figures the proof does not cover: a triangle whose corners are in a line, two points that coincide, two lines that were supposed to meet but are parallel. A textbook proof assumes these away silently. Here they are computed, and `proof.conditions` lists them with a geometric reading where one is recognised.

```js
import { proofs } from "@ratmath/geo";

const p = proofs.eulerLine().parts[0];         // O, G, H are collinear
String(p.identity.multiplier);                 // "b·d"   for A = (0, 0), B = (b, 0), C = (c, d)
p.identity.cofactors.map(String);              // the six cᵢ
p.conditions.map((c) => c.meaning);            // ["A, B, C are not collinear"]
p.explain();                                   // the whole proof as text
```

So the Euler line theorem is proved for every triangle that is not flat, which is every triangle.

### Wu's method

Build the figure one point at a time, and each new unknown coordinate arrives with the hypothesis that pins it down. The hypotheses are then in triangular form: h1​ involves the first unknown, h2​ the first two, and so on. Wu Wen-tsün's method divides the conclusion by the hypotheses in reverse order, each time treating the hypothesis as a polynomial in the unknown it introduced.

Division by a polynomial whose leading coefficient is itself a polynomial needs pseudo-division: multiply by that leading coefficient first, so that no fractions appear.

Is⋅g=q⋅h+r,degx​r<degx​h,
where I is the leading coefficient of h as a polynomial in x. If after dividing by every hypothesis the remainder is zero, the pieces assemble into the identity above, with d a product of leading coefficients. The method is fast, because it never does more than follow the construction backwards. Every theorem in the list on this page is proved this way in a few milliseconds, except Desargues' theorem, which takes about a third of a second.

When a point is given by two conditions that both involve both of its coordinates (the intersection of two lines, say), the library first eliminates one coordinate between them, again by pseudo-division, and keeps track of how the new polynomials are built from the original hypotheses, so that the final identity is still in terms of those.

### The Gröbner method

The second method follows Kapur. Treat the parameters as constants, that is, work with polynomials in the unknowns whose coefficients are rational functions of the parameters. The conclusion follows from the hypotheses, for general values of the parameters, exactly when

1∈⟨h1​,…,hr​, 1−tg⟩
for a new variable t. (If the hypotheses hold and g=0, the last generator is 1; if they hold and g=0, choose t=1/g. So the generators have no common zero exactly when g vanishes wherever the hypotheses do. This is Rabinowitsch's trick, the same one that proves the Nullstellensatz.) A [Gröbner basis](https://ratmath.com/structures/groebner.html) decides the question, and its cofactors, with denominators cleared and t replaced by 1/g, are the identity. The multiplier d is then a polynomial in the parameters alone, so the degenerate cases are conditions on the given points only.

```js
const w = proofs.simson({ method: "wu" });
const k = proofs.simson({ method: "groebner" });
[w.proved, k.proved];                          // [true, true]
k.conditions.map((c) => c.meaning);            // ["A, B, C are not collinear", "A ≠ C", "B ≠ C"]
[w.size.cofactorTerms, k.size.cofactorTerms];  // the two certificates differ, and both multiply out
```

The Gröbner method is complete where Wu's simple form is not: it finds a proof whenever the statement holds for general parameters. It is also much slower when the hypotheses are not linear in the unknowns, since it computes with fractions of polynomials. With `method: "auto"` (the default) Wu's method goes first; if it fails, one figure with random whole-number parameters is tried; and only if the conclusion holds at every solution of that figure is the Gröbner method run, with a time limit.

### What algebra cannot see

Polynomial equations do not distinguish inside from outside or one side of a line from the other. Three consequences are worth knowing.

- Bisectors. The condition "equal angles" describes the internal and the external bisector together. A point on a bisector at A and a bisector at B is the incentre or one of the three excentres; tritangentCenter means all four. Theorems true of all four (the third bisector passes through, the distances to the sides are equal) are proved. Theorems true only of the incentre are not, and the report says at how many of the solutions the conclusion held.

- Second intersections. "A point on this line and on this circle" has two solutions, and if one of them is already in the figure, the algebra allows the new point to be the old one. Use otherIntersection, which asks for the second point by a linear condition. The butterfly theorem is proved when stated that way and fails when stated loosely, as it should.

- Complex figures. The identity holds for complex coordinates too. That is usually harmless, but it means a statement can be true of all real figures and still not provable this way, if it fails for complex ones.

When no proof exists the result has `proved: false` and an `instance`: the parameters tried, the number of solutions of the hypotheses there, and at how many the conclusion holds. A statement that is simply false shows 0.

```js
const T = configuration("a false statement");
const A = T.at("A", 0, 0), B = T.at("B", "b", 0), C = T.at("C", "c", "d");
const M = T.midpoint("M", B, C);
const no = T.prove(T.perpendicular(A, M, B, C));     // "every median is an altitude"
no.proved;          // false
no.instance;        // { parameters: { b: 14, c: 13, d: 22 }, solutions: 1, holdsAt: 0 }
```

### Stating your own theorem

A configuration is built from points. The predicates return polynomials, and serve both as conditions on a new point and as conclusions.

| Points | meaning |

| T.at(name, x, y) | given coordinates: numbers, names of parameters (made on first use), or expressions |

| T.free(name) | both coordinates are parameters |

| T.on(name, P => condition, { free }) | one coordinate free, the other tied down by one condition |

| T.where(name, P => [c1, c2]) | both coordinates tied down by two conditions |

| T.parameter(name), T.unknown(name, v => condition) | a free number; a number defined by an equation, such as s with s² = 3 |

| midpoint, intersection, foot, reflection, parallelogram | constructions: T.intersection("P", [A, B], [C, D]) |

| circumcenter, orthocenter, centroid, tritangentCenter | triangle centres |

| onLine, onCircumcircle, otherIntersection | points on a line or circle |

| Predicates and quantities | vanishes when |

| collinear(A, B, C), concurrent(l1, l2, l3) | three points on a line; three lines through a point |

| parallel(A, B, C, D), perpendicular(A, B, C, D) | AB ∥ CD; AB ⊥ CD |

| equidistant(P, A, B), equalLength(A, B, C, D) | \|PA\| = \|PB\|; \|AB\| = \|CD\| |

| onCircle(P, O, A), concyclic(A, B, C, D), tangent(l, O, P) | circles |

| rightAngle(A, B, C), equalAngle(A, B, C, D, E, F) | angles, as angles between lines |

| isMidpoint(M, A, B) | two polynomials |

| distance2, area2, dot, cross, equal(a, b) | build your own: T.equal(T.distance2(A, B), T.distance2(C, D).mul(4)) |

### The theorems proved

`provable` lists them, and `proofs.<id>(options)` proves one. `proofs.setup(id)` hands back the configuration and conclusion for inspection.

| proofs.… | statement |

### Try it

```js
// A theorem that is not in the list: reflect the orthocentre H in the midpoint of BC.
// The image is on the circumcircle, and is the point opposite A.
const T = configuration("antipode");
const A = T.at("A", 0, 0), B = T.at("B", "b", 0), C = T.at("C", "c", "d");
const H = T.orthocenter("H", A, B, C);
const O = T.circumcenter("O", A, B, C);
const M = T.midpoint("M", B, C);
const K = T.where("K", (P) => T.isMidpoint(M, H, P), "M is the midpoint of HK");
const proof = T.prove([T.concyclic(A, B, C, K), T.isMidpoint(O, A, K)]);
PRINT(String(proof), " replayed:", proof.replay(), " in", proof.ms, "ms");
PRINT("degenerate cases:", proof.conditions.map((c) => c.meaning ?? c.text).join("; "));
PRINT(proof.parts[0].explain({ cofactors: false }));

// A statement that is true of some solutions only: a centre I on two bisectors, with |IA| = |IB|.
const U = configuration("isosceles?");
const P = U.at("A", 0, 0), Q = U.at("B", "b", 0), R = U.at("C", "c", "d");
const I = U.tritangentCenter("I", P, Q, R);
const bad = U.prove(U.equidistant(I, P, Q));
PRINT(String(bad), JSON.stringify(bad.instance));

// Every theorem in the library, with its method and time
proofs.all().map(({ name, proof }) => `${name}: ${proof.proved ? "proved" : "NOT proved"} (${proof.method}, ${proof.ms} ms)`)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/conics.html

Topic

## Conic sections

Give `conicProperties` any equation Ax2+Bxy+Cy2+Dx+Ey+F=0 and it says what the curve is and finds everything a course asks about it: the centre or vertex, the axes, vertices, foci, eccentricity, directrices and asymptotes. The answers are exact, square roots and all, even when the conic is turned by an angle that is not a nice one.

### What kind of conic

Two numbers decide it. The determinant Δ of the symmetric matrix ​AB/2D/2​B/2CE/2​D/2E/2F​​ says whether the conic is degenerate, and the discriminant B2−4AC says which shape it has:

| | B2−4AC0 |

| Δ=0 | ellipse (circle when A=C, B=0), or empty when (A+C)Δ>0 | parabola | hyperbola |

| Δ=0 | a single point | two parallel lines, a double line, or empty | two crossing lines |

A degenerate or empty conic returns its type and nothing more.

### Centre and axes

An ellipse or hyperbola has a centre, where the gradient of the left side vanishes: a 2 × 2 linear system. Moving the centre to the origin leaves λ1​X2+λ2​Y2+F′=0 in the directions of the eigenvectors of (AB/2​B/2C​), with F′=Δ/(AC−B2/4). Then a2=−F′/λ along the axis whose λ is smaller in size (for a hyperbola, the one whose λ has the sign of −F′), and c2=a2∓b2. With B=0 the axes are the coordinate directions and everything is rational or one square root; with B=0 the eigenvalues are square roots and the directions are algebraic numbers, still exact.

```js
const e = conicProperties("9x^2 + 4y^2 - 36 = 0");
e.type;          // "ellipse"
e.a; e.b;        // 3, 2
e.foci;          // [(0, √5), (0, −√5)]
e.eccentricity;  // √5/3

const h = conicProperties("x^2/16 - y^2/9 = 1");
h.asymptotes;    // ["3·x − 4·y = 0", "3·x + 4·y = 0"]
h.directrices;   // ["5·x − 16 = 0", "5·x + 16 = 0"]: x = ±a²/c

conicProperties("x^2 + xy + y^2 = 3").axes.major;   // x + y = 0, with a² = 6, b² = 2
```

### Parabolas

When B2=4AC the quadratic part is a perfect square and one eigenvalue is 0; its eigenvector is the direction of the axis. In coordinates along and across the axis the equation becomes (w−w0​)2=4p(s−s0​): the vertex is (s0​,w0​), the focus is p along the axis from it, and the directrix is p the other way.

```js
const p = conicProperties("x^2 - 4y - 2x + 9 = 0");
p.vertex;      // (1, 2)
p.focus;       // (1, 3)
p.directrix;   // y − 1 = 0
conicProperties("x^2 - 2xy + y^2 - 4x - 4y = 0").focus;   // (1/2, 1/2): a parabola turned 45°
```

A projective `Conic` (see [the projective plane](https://ratmath.com/geo/projective.html)) has the same answers through `conic.properties()`, and [`circleFromEquation`](https://ratmath.com/geo/measurement.html) is the circle case.

### Try it

```js
// An ellipse turned by the 3-4-5 rotation and moved to (1, −2): X²/25 + Y²/9 = 1
const e = conicProperties("(3(x-1) + 4(y+2))^2/625 + (-4(x-1) + 3(y+2))^2/225 = 1");
PRINT(e.type, " centre", String(e.center), " a =", String(e.a), " b =", String(e.b), " foci", e.foci.map(String).join(" "));

// The focal property: from every point of the curve the distances to the foci add to 2a = 10
for (const P of [...e.vertices, ...e.coVertices]) PRINT(String(P), "→", String(N.add(distance(P, e.foci[0]), distance(P, e.foci[1]))));

// A hyperbola and its asymptotes
const h = conicProperties("x^2/16 - y^2/9 = 1");
PRINT("eccentricity", String(h.eccentricity), " asymptotes", h.asymptotes.map(String).join(", "));

// Degenerate cases stop at their type
for (const t of ["x^2 - y^2 = 0", "x^2 + y^2 = 0", "x^2 = 1", "x^2 + y^2 + 1 = 0"]) PRINT(t, "→", conicProperties(t).type);
conicProperties("x^2 - 2xy + y^2 - 4x - 4y = 0").directrix
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/space.html

Topic

## Vectors, lines and planes in space

Three-dimensional coordinates, exact: the dot and cross products, lengths that stay square roots, angles, projections, and the lines and planes of multivariable calculus with their equations, distances and intersections.

### Vectors

`vector(x, y, z)` takes rationals or exact numbers such as `"sqrt(2)"`. The dot product u⋅v=u1​v1​+u2​v2​+u3​v3​ is ∣u∣∣v∣cosθ; the cross product

u×v=(u2​v3​−u3​v2​, u3​v1​−u1​v3​, u1​v2​−u2​v1​)
is perpendicular to both, with length ∣u∣∣v∣sinθ, the area of the parallelogram they span. The scalar triple product u⋅(v×w) is the signed volume of the parallelepiped.

```js
const u = vector(1, 2, -2), v = vector(3, 0, 4);
u.dot(v);          // -5
u.cross(v);        // (8, -10, -6)
u.norm;            // 3
u.angle(v).cos;    // -1/3
v.projectOnto([0, 0, 1]);              // (0, 0, 4)
tripleProduct([4, 0, 0], [0, 5, 0], [0, 0, 6]);   // 120
```

### Planes

A plane is n⋅x=d for a normal n. Through three points P,Q,R the normal is (Q−P)×(R−P), and three points on one line are refused. The equation prints with whole coefficients and no common factor. The distance from a point is ∣n⋅p−d∣/∣n∣, reached at the foot of the perpendicular.

```js
const P = plane([1, 0, 2], [2, 1, 0], [0, 3, 1]);
P.equation;            // "5x + 3y + 4z = 13"
P.distance([0, 0, 0]); // 13/√50, an exact square root
P.foot([0, 0, 0]);     // (13/10, 39/50, 26/25)
plane([0, 0, 0], { normal: [0, 0, 1] });   // z = 0
plane({ coefficients: [1, 1, 1, 3] });     // x + y + z = 3
```

### Lines and intersections

`line3(p, q)` is the line p+t(q−p). A plane meets a line in a point (or contains it, or misses it), and two planes that are not parallel meet in a line whose direction is the cross product of their normals.

```js
const Q = plane({ coefficients: [1, -1, 0, 1] });
plane({ coefficients: [1, 1, 1, 3] }).meet(Q);    // a Line3: point + t·(1, 1, -2)
P.meet(line3([0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1]));              // (13/12, 13/12, 13/12)
```

### Try it

```js
const u = vector(1, 2, -2), v = vector(3, 0, 4);
PRINT("u·v =", String(u.dot(v)), " u×v =", String(u.cross(v)), " |u| =", String(u.norm), " |v| =", String(v.norm));
PRINT("angle between u and v:", u.angle(v).degrees.toFixed(4), "degrees");
// the cross product is perpendicular to both, and |u×v|² = |u|²|v|² − (u·v)²
const w = u.cross(v);
PRINT("perpendicular:", w.isOrthogonal(u), w.isOrthogonal(v), " Lagrange:", String(w.norm2), "=", String(u.norm2.multiply(v.norm2).subtract(u.dot(v).multiply(u.dot(v)))));

// The plane through three points, and the distance to the origin
const P = plane([1, 0, 2], [2, 1, 0], [0, 3, 1]);
PRINT(P.equation, " distance from the origin:", String(P.distance([0, 0, 0])));

// Where two planes cross
const L = P.meet(plane([0, 0, 0], { normal: [0, 0, 1] }));
PRINT("meets z = 0 along", String(L));
P.foot([0, 0, 0])
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/computational.html

Topic

## Hulls, triangulations and Voronoi diagrams

The algorithms of computational geometry are built from two questions: is this a left turn, and is this point inside that circle? Asked in floating point they sometimes get the wrong answer, and the algorithm then loops or returns nonsense. Asked exactly they cannot.

```js
convexHull(points);                       // counter-clockwise, edge points dropped
const p = polygon([[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 3], [2, 1], [0, 3]]);
p.area; p.centroid; p.isSimple(); p.isConvex();
p.locate([2, 1]);                         // "boundary": decided exactly
p.triangulate();                          // [[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 3], [0, 3, 4]]
p.clip([[1, 1], [5, 1], [5, 5], [1, 5]]); // intersection with a convex polygon
delaunay(points);                         // { points, triangles, edges, cocircular }
voronoi(points);                          // { vertices, cells, edges }
```

### The two predicates

Orientation. For points p, q, r the sign of the cross product (q−p)×(r−p) is +1 for a left turn, −1 for a right turn and 0 when the three are collinear. Convex hulls, segment intersection and point-in-polygon tests use nothing else.

In-circle. Whether d is inside the circle through a, b, c is the sign of a 3×3 determinant in the coordinates. Delaunay triangulations are defined by it: no point may lie inside the circle through the corners of any triangle.

Both are signs of polynomials, and with rational coordinates they are computed without error. The value 0 (three points on a line, four on a circle) is a real answer here and is handled as a case: the hull drops points on its edges, `locate` answers `"boundary"`, and `delaunay` reports `cocircular: true` when the triangulation is not unique.

### Polygons

The area is the shoelace formula and the centroid its companion, both exact. `isSimple()` tests every pair of edges for crossings. `triangulate()` clips ears: a corner whose triangle contains no other vertex is cut off, and this repeats. `clip(convex)` cuts the polygon by each edge of a convex polygon in turn (Sutherland and Hodgman's method); the new corners are intersections of lines with rational coefficients, so they are rational.

### Delaunay and Voronoi

`delaunay` adds the points one at a time: the triangles whose circles contain the new point are removed and the hole is re-triangulated from the new point (Bowyer and Watson's method). `voronoi` is the dual picture: each point's cell is the set of places nearer to it than to any other point, and its corners are the circumcentres of the Delaunay triangles around that point, which are rational when the points are. Cells of points on the hull are unbounded; their open edges are returned as rays.

| call | returns |

| convexHull(points) | Point[] |

| segmentIntersection(a, b, c, d), onSegment(a, b, p) | { meets, kind, point }; boolean |

| polygon(vertices) | Polygon: area, signedArea, perimeter, centroid, edges |

| p.isSimple(), p.isConvex(), p.locate(q), p.contains(q) | "inside" \| "boundary" \| "outside" |

| p.triangulate(), p.clip(convex) | index triples; Polygon or null |

| inCircle(a, b, c, d) | 1 inside, 0 on, −1 outside |

| delaunay(points) | { points, triangles, edges, cocircular } |

| voronoi(points) | { points, vertices, cells: [{ site, corners, bounded }], edges } |

| closestPair(points) | { points, distance, distance2 } |

### Try it

```js
const pts = [[0, 0], [4, 0], [0, 3], [4, 3], [2, 1], [1, 2], [3, 5], [2, 0]];
PRINT("hull:", convexHull(pts).join(" "));
const d = delaunay(pts);
PRINT("Delaunay triangles:", d.triangles.map((t) => t.join("-")).join("  "), " cocircular:", d.cocircular);
const empty = d.triangles.every(([a, b, c]) => d.points.every((p, i) => [a, b, c].includes(i) || inCircle(d.points[a], d.points[b], d.points[c], p) <= 0));
PRINT("every circle is empty:", empty);
const v = voronoi(pts);
for (const cell of v.cells.filter((c) => c.bounded)) PRINT("cell of", String(cell.site), "has corners", cell.corners.join(" "));

const p = polygon([[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 3], [2, 1], [0, 3]]);
PRINT("area", N.text(p.area), " centroid", String(p.centroid), " simple", p.isSimple(), " convex", p.isConvex());
PRINT("(2, 1) is", p.locate([2, 1]), " (2, 2) is", p.locate([2, 2]), " (1, 1) is", p.locate([1, 1]));
PRINT("triangles:", p.triangulate().map((t) => t.join("-")).join("  "));
PRINT("a square's Delaunay triangulation is not unique:", delaunay([[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]).cocircular);
String(p.clip([[1, 1], [5, 1], [5, 5], [1, 5]]))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/lattice.html

Topic

## Lattice points and Pick's theorem

The points with whole-number coordinates form a lattice, and polygons with corners on it have areas that can be found by counting.

```js
pick([[0, 0], [5, 0], [0, 5]]);     // { area: 25/2, interior: 6, boundary: 15, formula: 25/2, holds: true }
latticePointsOn([0, 0], [6, 4]);    // 3: the ends and (3, 2)
isVisible(3, 5);                    // true: gcd(3, 5) = 1
visiblePoints(100);                 // { count: 6087, share: 6087/10000, … }
```

### Pick's theorem

For a polygon whose corners are lattice points and whose edges do not cross, with I lattice points strictly inside and B on the boundary,

area=I+2B​−1.
`pick` finds the three quantities independently, so that `holds` is a check and not a restatement. The area comes from the shoelace formula. B comes from the edges: the segment from (0, 0) to (a, b) passes through gcd(a, b) + 1 lattice points, since the first one after the origin is (a/g, b/g). I is counted by testing every lattice point of the bounding box with the exact point-in-polygon test.

The theorem fails for polygons with holes and has no analogue in three dimensions: a tetrahedron with corners (0,0,0), (1,0,0), (0,1,0), (1,1,n) contains no other lattice points, yet its volume n/6 can be as large as you like.

### Visible points

From the origin, the lattice point (x, y) is visible when no other lattice point lies on the segment to it, which is when gcd(x, y) = 1. The share of visible points in a large square tends to

ζ(2)1​=π26​≈0.6079,
because two numbers avoid sharing the prime factor p with probability 1−1/p2, and the product of these over all primes is 1/ζ(2). `visiblePoints(n)` gives the exact count in the n by n square and its share as a fraction; that the share approaches 6/π2 is a limit it illustrates and does not prove.

| call | returns |

| pick(vertices \| polygon) | { area, interior, boundary, formula, holds } |

| latticePointsOn(p, q) | number of lattice points on the closed segment |

| isVisible(x, y) | boolean |

| visiblePoints(n) | { n, count, share, limit } |

### Try it

```js
for (const v of [[[0, 0], [5, 0], [0, 5]], [[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 3], [2, 1], [0, 3]], [[0, 0], [7, 1], [9, 6], [3, 8], [-2, 4]]]) {
  const r = pick(v);
  PRINT(`area ${N.text(r.area)} = ${r.interior} + ${r.boundary}/2 − 1 = ${N.text(r.formula)}  → ${r.holds}`);
}
PRINT("lattice points from (0,0) to (12, 18):", latticePointsOn([0, 0], [12, 18]));
for (const n of [10, 100, 1000]) {
  const v = visiblePoints(n);
  PRINT(`n = ${n}: ${v.count} visible, share ${v.share.toNumber().toFixed(4)}`);
}
"6/π² = " + (6 / Math.PI ** 2).toFixed(6)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/metrics.html

Topic

## Other ways to measure distance

Change how distance is measured and the plane is the same set of points with a different geometry. In a city of square blocks the distance that matters is ∣dx∣+∣dy∣, and circles turn into squares.

```js
const taxi = metric("taxicab");          // also "chebyshev" (max(|dx|, |dy|)) and "euclidean"
taxi.distance([0, 0], [3, 4]);           // 7
taxi.circle([0, 0], 2);                  // the corners (2,0), (0,2), (−2,0), (0,−2)
taxi.pi;                                 // 4
taxi.bisector([0, 0], [4, 2]);           // a bent line: { segments, rays, regions, kind }
taxi.ellipse([0, 0], [4, 0], 6);         // six corners
```

### Circles and π

A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from a centre. In the taxicab metric ∣x∣+∣y∣=r is a square standing on a corner; in the Chebyshev metric max(∣x∣,∣y∣)=r is a square with level sides. Measuring the circumference in the same metric and dividing by the diameter gives 4 in both, so "π = 4" there. The two metrics are in fact the same geometry turned by 45° and rescaled, and `ellipse` for the Chebyshev metric is computed through that change of coordinates.

### Bisectors

The points equally far from P and Q form a straight line in Euclid's geometry. In taxicab geometry the middle part is a segment of slope ±1, and it continues from each end as a vertical ray (when P and Q are further apart sideways than up and down) or a horizontal one. When ∣dx∣=∣dy∣ something stranger happens: beyond each end of the diagonal segment an entire quarter of the plane is equidistant from the two points. `bisector` returns the segment, the rays and, in that case, the two regions by their corner and bounding directions.

One consequence: the theorem that three points not on a line have exactly one point equidistant from all of them fails. Three such points can have none, or infinitely many.

### Ellipses

The points whose distances to two foci add up to a constant form a hexagon or an octagon. `ellipse` returns its corners, found exactly: the sum of distances is a convex function that is linear between the vertical and horizontal lines through the foci, so the corners lie on those lines.

### Side-angle-side fails

Congruence fails too. The triangle (0,0), (2,0), (0,2) and the triangle (0,0), (1,1), (1,−1) each have two sides of taxicab length 2 from the origin with a right angle between them, yet the third sides have taxicab lengths 4 and 2. Side-angle-side is not a theorem here, and taxicab geometry is the standard example of a geometry that satisfies Euclid's other axioms without it.

| call | returns |

| metric(name).distance(p, q) | exact number |

| .circle(centre, r) | the four corners |

| .pi | circumference ÷ diameter in that metric |

| .bisector(p, q) (taxicab) | { segments, rays, regions, kind } |

| .ellipse(f1, f2, sum) | the corners, counter-clockwise |

### Try it

```js
const taxi = metric("taxicab");
const cheb = metric("chebyshev");
const eu = metric("euclidean");
PRINT("from (0,0) to (3,4): taxicab", N.text(taxi.distance([0, 0], [3, 4])), " Chebyshev", N.text(cheb.distance([0, 0], [3, 4])), " Euclid", N.text(eu.distance([0, 0], [3, 4])));
PRINT("taxicab circle:", taxi.circle([0, 0], 2).join(" "), "  π =", N.text(taxi.pi));
const b = taxi.bisector([0, 0], [4, 2]);
PRINT("bisector of (0,0) and (4,2):", b.kind + ":", "segment", b.segments[0].join(" to "), "then rays", b.rays.map((r) => `from ${r.from} towards ${r.direction}`).join(" and "));
PRINT("bisector of (0,0) and (2,2):", taxi.bisector([0, 0], [2, 2]).kind);
PRINT("ellipse, foci (0,0) and (4,0), sum 6:", taxi.ellipse([0, 0], [4, 0], 6).join(" "));
PRINT("ellipse, foci (0,0) and (2,2), sum 6:", taxi.ellipse([0, 0], [2, 2], 6).join(" "));
// side-angle-side fails: two triangles with a right angle between sides of taxicab length 2
const d = (p, q) => N.text(taxi.distance(p, q));
`third sides: ${d([2, 0], [0, 2])} and ${d([1, 1], [1, -1])}`
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/spherical.html

Topic

## Spherical geometry

On a sphere the straight lines are the great circles. Any two of them cross, the angles of a triangle add up to more than two right angles, and the surplus is the triangle's area. Here the points have exact coordinates, so those statements are equalities, not measurements.

```js
const A = spoint(1, 0, 0), B = spoint(1, 1, 0), C = spoint(1, 1, 1);   // any non-zero vector, scaled onto the sphere
A.distanceTo(B).text;                     // "π/4": the distance is the angle between them
const t = striangle(A, B, C);
[t.angles.A.text, t.angles.B.text, t.angles.C.text];   // ["π/4", "π/2", "π/3"]
t.excess.text;                            // "π/12": the angle sum is π + π/12
String(t.fractionOfSphere);               // "1/48"
t.checks().all;                           // true: every law of spherical trigonometry, exactly
greatCircle(A, B).meet(greatCircle(A, C));   // two opposite points: there are no parallels
```

### Points and distance

A point is a unit vector (x,y,z) with x2+y2+z2=1, and the coordinates are exact real algebraic numbers. `spoint(1, 1, 1)` scales a vector onto the sphere, giving (33​​,33​​,33​​); `latLon(lat, lon)` takes a latitude and longitude as fractions of a full turn; and `fromStereographic([X, Y])` lifts a point of the plane, which turns rational points of the plane into rational points of the sphere, such as (4936​,4924​,−4923​).

The distance between two points is the angle between the vectors, measured along the great circle through them, and its cosine is the dot product:

cosd(P,Q)=P⋅Q.
The cosine is exact. The distance itself is an `Angle`.

### Angles that are, and are not, fractions of π

An `Angle` keeps its cosine and sine exactly. Its `turns` is the angle as a fraction of a full turn when it is a rational multiple of π, and `null` when it is not, and the answer is decided, not guessed. The reason it can be decided: cos(2πk/n) is an algebraic number of degree φ(n)/2 (Euler's function), so the degree of a cosine leaves only finitely many denominators n to try, and each is tested with an exact equality. In particular a rational cosine can only be 0,±21​,±1 (Niven's theorem), so the angle with cosine 31​ is not a rational multiple of π, and the library says so with a proof behind it.

When the angle is such a multiple, `text` is of the form "π/12". Otherwise `value(digits)` gives an interval of radians that contains it. Angles add as real numbers (a float tracks which turn the sum is on), so an angle sum of 13π/12 is that and not the same thing modulo 2π.

### Great circles

A great circle is where a plane through the centre cuts the sphere. It is kept as a vector n normal to that plane: the circle is {P:n⋅P=0}. Through two points that are neither equal nor opposite there is exactly one, with n=P×Q. Two great circles always meet, in the two opposite points ±n1​×n2​. So on the sphere there are no parallel lines, and two "lines" meet twice, which is why two points do not always determine a line: through two opposite points there are infinitely many, and `greatCircle` refuses them.

### Triangles and their excess

Three points not on one great circle make a triangle. Its sides a,b,c are angles (the distances between the vertices), and its angles A,B,C are the angles between the planes of the sides. Their sum is always more than π, and the surplus

E=A+B+C−π
is the spherical excess. Girard's theorem says the area of the triangle on the unit sphere is exactly E. The octant triangle with vertices on the three axes has three right angles, excess π/2, and covers one eighth of the sphere's 4π. The triangle in the example at the top has angles π/4,π/2,π/3 and covers one forty-eighth: the 48 symmetries of a cube move it over the whole sphere.

When the angles are not fractions of π the excess usually is not one either, and it comes as an enclosure. `checks()` also tests it against a formula that needs no angles at all,

tan2E​=1+A⋅B+B⋅C+C⋅A∣A⋅(B×C)∣​,
as an exact equality of algebraic numbers.

### Spherical trigonometry

The plane's law of cosines has two forms on the sphere:

cosa=cosbcosc+sinbsinccosA,cosA=−cosBcosC+sinBsinCcosa.
The second has no counterpart in the plane: it gives the sides from the angles, so on a sphere there are no similar triangles of different sizes. The law of sines is sinA/sina=sinB/sinb=sinC/sinc. The polar triangle, whose vertices are the poles of the sides, has sides π−A,π−B,π−C. `checks()` tests all of these on the triangle given, each as an exact equality.

### Circles

A circle of radius r (an angle) about a point has circumference 2πsinr and encloses a cap of area 2π(1−cosr): both less than the plane's 2πr and πr2. They come as exact multiples of π: the circle of radius π/6 has circumference exactly π and area (2−3​)π.

### Isometries

The isometries of the sphere are the orthogonal 3 × 3 matrices. `srotation(axis, turns)` is the rotation about an axis, and `classify()` reads any isometry back: by Euler's theorem every isometry that keeps orientation is a rotation about some axis, so the product of two rotations about different axes is a third rotation, and the library finds its axis and angle exactly. The ones that reverse orientation are reflections in great circles and rotary reflections, the antipodal map among them.

| call | returns |

| spoint(x, y, z), latLon(lat, lon), fromStereographic(p), northPole() | SPoint: x, y, z, antipode, distanceTo, dot, latLon, stereographic |

| greatCircle(P, Q), greatCircle(pole), equator() | GreatCircle: contains, side, poles, meet, angleWith, perpendicularThrough, distanceTo, reflection, parallelsThrough |

| striangle(A, B, C) | STriangle: sides, angles, angleSum, excess, area, fractionOfSphere, perimeter, polar, classify(), checks() |

| scircle(centre, point \| { radius } \| { cos }) | SCircle: radius, circumference, area, contains, isGreat |

| srotation(axis, turns), antipodalMap(), circle.reflection | SIsometry: apply, then, inverse, classify() |

| angle(turns \| { cos } \| { cos, sin }), Angle | cos, sin, turns, text, degrees, value(digits), add, sub, equals |

| turnsOfCos(c), piTimes(k), lune(angle) | The fraction of a turn with that cosine, or null; π times an exact number; a lune's area |

### Try it

```js
const t = striangle([1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 0], [1, 1, 1]);
PRINT("angles:", t.angles.A.text, t.angles.B.text, t.angles.C.text, "  sides:", t.sides.a.text, t.sides.b.text, t.sides.c.text);
PRINT("excess:", t.excess.text, "  share of the sphere:", String(t.fractionOfSphere));
PRINT("laws:", JSON.stringify(t.checks()));
// a triangle with no nice angle: still exact cosines, and the excess enclosed
const u = striangle([1, 2, 2], [2, -1, 2], [0, 0, 1]);
PRINT("cos A =", N.text(u.angles.A.cos), " A =", u.angles.A.text, " a fraction of π?", u.angles.A.isRational);
PRINT("excess in", u.excess.value(15).low.toDecimal(15), "…, laws hold:", u.checks().all);
// Niven: the angle with cosine 1/3 is not a rational multiple of π
PRINT("turnsOfCos(1/2) =", String(turnsOfCos("1/2")), "  turnsOfCos(1/3) =", String(turnsOfCos("1/3")));
// two quarter turns about different axes make a third of a turn
const r = srotation([0, 0, 1], "1/4").then(srotation([1, 0, 0], "1/4"));
PRINT(String(r));
const c = scircle([0, 0, 1], { radius: "1/12" });
`circle of radius π/6: circumference ${c.circumference.text}, area ${c.area.text}`
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/geo/hyperbolic.html

Topic

## The hyperbolic plane

In the hyperbolic plane, through a point off a line there are infinitely many lines that never meet it. The plane cannot be drawn in ours without distortion, so it is drawn in models, each wrong in a different way. Here a point is one exact object and the models are four views of it.

